newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Thuraya to award $1.2 bln satellite deal in month.
newsitem.headline: Thuraya to award $1.2 bln satellite deal in month.

text.p: A new Abu Dhabi-based communications firm said on Monday it planned to announce within a month the winner of a $1.2 billion deal for a satellite system to extend mobile telecommunications throughout the Arab world.

Thuraya Satellite Telecommunications Co Chairman Mohammad Hassan Omran told a news conference the company had received final bids from three international firms to design, construct and launch a satellite system by the year 2000 to mainly cover Arab states and the Indian subcontinent.
In the race to supply Thuraya, which in Arabic means the Pleiades or Taurus star cluster, are U.S. firms Hughes and Lockheed Martin and France's Aerospatiale.
"We estimate that over 12 years the cost of the project will be $1.2 billion," Thuraya Project Manager Yousuf al-Sayed said.

Omran said the offers were being scrutinised by Thuraya's executive committee. "(It) will present its recommendations to a meeting of the board of directors on August 26 for selecting the suitable system supplier," he added.
The board would then announce the preferred bidder, Sayed said, to go into the last round of negotiations with Thuraya.
"These should finish by September 9 and on September 10 the board will authorise the chairman to ink the deal, with the signing due to take place on September 11," Sayed said.
Thuraya plans to provide mobile communication services based on a satellite system launched into orbit over the Indian Ocean.
It will extend the reach of mobile phones in Arab countries, Iran, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Central Asia, Turkey and parts of Europe, making services available to remote sea and rural areas.
"We have a requirement for one satellite in orbit and one as a ground spare. We will launch the second satellite two to three years after the first if there is enough demand," Sayed said.
The first satellite was conservatively forecast to have capacity to handle 1.75 million subscribers, a total which was expected to be reached within four or five years.
"The less-conservative forecast is 2.4 million subscribers on a single satellite. We can also add another 40 percent capacity with a second satellite," Sayed said.
Chairman Omran said 10 companies had so far committed to taking stakes totalling more than 75 percent in Thuraya, which will be capitalised at $500 million.
Talks were being held with other potential investors, whose stakes Omran hoped would be confirmed by month-end.
"We plan also to allocate five percent of the capital to the successful supplier," Omran said.

UAE telecommunications company Etisalat will be the biggest shareholder with 26 percent. Abu Dhabi Investment Co will follow with a 20 percent stake, The Arab Satellite Communications Organisation (Arabsat) -- owned by 21 Arab countries -- and Qatar's state-owned Q-Tel will each take 10 percent.
Dubai Investment Co and Gulf Investment Corp will own a respective five and two percent of Thuraya's shares.

Bahrain Telecommunications Co and Kuwait's Mobile Telephone Co have each committed to take one percent. Egypt's National Telecommunications Organisation (ARENTO) and Deutsche Telekom GmbH unit DeTeCon of Germany will hold 0.65 and 0.5 percent respectively.
